motion_text:
Council Decision

MOVED by Councillor Kirby-Yung
SECONDED by Councillor Klassen

A. THAT the application by Vancouver Harbour Flight Centre Ltd., on behalf of the
B.C. Pavilion Corporation, the registered owner of the lands located at 1055-
1085 Canada Place and 1001-1045 West Waterfront Road [PID 027-112-721;
Parcel 1 of the Public Harbour Burrard Inlet Plan BCP30843 Except Plan

Public Hearing
Minutes, Tuesday, April 14, 2026 4

EPP2853] to amend CD-1 (Comprehensive Development) District (363) By-law
No. 7679 to increase the maximum floor area of sub-area 2 from 98,122 sq. m
(1,056,176 sq. ft.) to 101,223 sq. m (1,089,555 sq. ft.) and increase the maximum
height for structures between the Vancouver Convention and Exhibition Centre
and the harbour headline from 9.0 m (30 ft.) to 20.0 m (66 ft.), to permit a 250-
room floating hotel and a new dock at water level with a public walkway and
commercial uses, generally as presented in the Referral Report dated
March 10, 2026, entitled “CD-1 (363) Text Amendment: 1055-1085 Canada
Place and 1001-1045 West Waterfront Road,” be approved in principle;

FURTHER THAT the draft by-law to amend CD-1 (363) By-law No. 7679,
prepared for the Public Hearing in accordance with Appendix A of the above-
noted report, be approved in principle;

FURTHER THAT the proposed form of development also be approved in
principle, generally as prepared by Dialog, received December 23, 2024;

FURTHER THAT the above approvals be subject to the Conditions of Approval
contained in Appendix B of the above-noted report;

AND FURTHER THAT the staff yellow memorandum dated April 7, 2026, entitled
“CD-1 (363) Text Amendment: 1055-1085 Canada Place and 1001-1045 West
Waterfront Road – Amend Report Text,” form a part of this motion.

B. THAT A above be adopted on the following conditions:

(i) THAT the passage of the above resolutions creates no legal rights for the
applicant or any other person, or obligation on the part of the City; and
any expenditure of funds or incurring of costs is at the risk of the person
making the expenditure or incurring the cost;

(ii) THAT any approval that may be granted following the Public Hearing
shall not obligate the City to enact a by-law rezoning the property, and
any costs incurred in fulfilling requirements imposed as a condition of
rezoning are at the risk of the property owner; and

(iii) THAT the City and all its officials, including the Approving Officer, shall
not in any way be limited or directed in the exercise of their authority or
discretion, regardless of when they are called upon to exercise such
authority or discretion.
summary: Approves additional floor area and height for a 250-room floating hotel, dock, public walkway and commercial uses.
rationale: The exact minutes excerpt clearly describes and approves the hotel and waterfront development.

agenda_description: RR1. Fast-Tracking Rental Housing and Small Hotels - New Mixed-Use Commercial District
motion_group_title: RR1. Fast-Tracking Rental Housing and Small Hotels - New Mixed-Use Commercial District
motion_text:
REFERRAL REPORTS

1. Fast-Tracking Rental Housing and Small Hotels – New Mixed-Use Commercial
District
March 3, 2026

THAT the General Manager of Planning, Urban Design and Sustainability be instructed
to bring forward the Rental Housing Stock Official Development Plan, Downtown
Eastside/Oppenheimer Official Development Plan, and rezoning applications and plans,
described below, and that the applications and plans be referred to Public Hearing
together with the recommendations set out below;

FURTHER THAT the Director of Legal Services be instructed to prepare the necessary
by-laws, in accordance with the recommendations set out below, for consideration at
Public Hearing, notwithstanding that rezoning application and plans are consistent with
the applicable Official Development Plans.

Recommendations for Council

A. THAT Council approve the application to amend the Zoning and Development
By-law in accordance with Appendix A of the Referral Report dated March 3,
2026, entitled “Fast-Tracking Rental Housing and Small Hotels – New Mixed-Use
Commercial District,” as follows:

(i) add a new commercial district schedule C-2A;
(ii) rezone certain parcels from C-2, C-2B, C-2C and C-2C1 districts to new
C-2A district; and
(iii) update wording for consistency of regulations;

FURTHER THAT the Director of Legal Services be instructed to bring forward for
enactment amendments to the Zoning and Development By-law generally in
accordance with Appendix A of the above-noted report.

Council Meeting
Minutes, April 14, 2026 21

B. THAT, subject to approval of A above, Council approve the amendments to the
Rental Housing Stock Official Development Plan By-law to include the C-2A
district generally in accordance with Appendix B of the Referral Report dated
March 3, 2026, entitled “Fast-Tracking Rental Housing and Small Hotels – New
Mixed-Use Commercial District”;

FURTHER THAT the Director of Legal Services be instructed to bring forward for
enactment amendments to the Rental Housing Stock Official Development Plan
By-law generally in accordance with Appendix B of the above-noted report at the
time of enactment of the Zoning and Development By-law amendments in A
above.

C. THAT, subject to approval of A above, Council approve the amendments to the
Subdivision By-law to include the C-2A district generally in accordance with
Appendix C of the Referral Report dated March 3, 2026, entitled “Fast-Tracking
Rental Housing and Small Hotels – New Mixed-Use Commercial District”;

FURTHER THAT the Director of Legal Services be instructed to bring forward for
enactment amendments to the Subdivision By-law generally in accordance with
Appendix C of the above-noted report at the time of enactment of the Zoning and
Development By-law amendments in A above.

D. THAT, subject to approval of A above, Council approve the amendments to the
Sign By-law to include the C-2A district generally in accordance with Appendix D
of the Referral Report dated March 3, 2026, entitled “Fast-Tracking Rental
Housing and Small Hotels – New Mixed-Use Commercial District”;

FURTHER THAT the Director of Legal Services be instructed to bring forward for
enactment amendments to the Sign By-law generally in accordance with
Appendix D of the above-noted report at the time of enactment of the Zoning and
Development By-law amendments in A above.

E. THAT, subject to approval of A above, Council approve the amendments to the
Noise Control By-law to include the C-2A district generally in accordance with
Appendix E of the Referral Report dated March 3, 2026, entitled “Fast-Tracking
Rental Housing and Small Hotels – New Mixed-Use Commercial District,”;

FURTHER THAT the Director of Legal Services be instructed to bring forward for
enactment amendments to the Noise Control By-law generally in accordance
with Appendix E of the above-noted report at the time of enactment of the Zoning
and Development By-law amendments in A above.

F. THAT, subject to approval of A above, Council approve the amendments to the
Parking By-law to include the C-2A district generally in accordance with Appendix
F of the Referral Report dated March 3, 2026, entitled “Fast-Tracking Rental
Housing and Small Hotels – New Mixed-Use Commercial District”;

FURTHER THAT the Director of Legal Services be instructed to bring forward for
enactment amendments to the Parking By-law generally in accordance with
Appendix F of the above-noted report at the time of enactment of the Zoning and
Development By-law amendments in A above.

Council Meeting
Minutes, April 14, 2026 22

G. THAT, subject to approval of A above, Council approve the amendments to the
Downtown Eastside/Oppenheimer Official Development Plan By-law to update
wording for consistency of regulations, generally in accordance with Appendix G
of the Referral Report dated March 3, 2026, entitled “Fast-Tracking Rental
Housing and Small Hotels – New Mixed-Use Commercial District”;

FURTHER THAT the Director of Legal Services be instructed to bring forward for
enactment amendments to the Downtown Eastside/Oppenheimer Official
Development Plan By-law generally in accordance with Appendix G of the
above-noted report at the time of enactment of the Zoning and Development
By-law amendments in A above.

H. THAT, at the time of enactment of the amendments to the Zoning and
Development By-law, Council approve the amendments to various land use
documents generally in accordance with Appendix H of the Referral Report dated
March 3, 2026, entitled “Fast-Tracking Rental Housing and Small Hotels – New
Mixed-Use Commercial District”.
summary: Advances a new mixed-use commercial district and related by-law changes intended to fast-track rental housing and small hotels.
rationale: The exact minutes excerpt details approval and referral of the new district and associated land-use amendments.

THAT WHEREAS section 219 of the Vancouver Charter requires that the Director of
Finance submit to Council each year the detailed estimates of revenues and
expenditures of the City for the year;

estimates of revenues and expenditures for the City as soon thereafter as possible after

$2,392,516,008;

appropriation requests of all departments and boards properly supported by detailed
analysis of those expenditures and listings of the salaried staff;

AND WHEREAS the total estimated revenue of the City for 2025 from sources other

AND WHEREAS the amount of the General Purposes Tax Levy so required is
$1,224,250,000;

agenda_description: R6. Coastal Flood Management Policy - Amendment
motion_group_title: R6. Coastal Flood Management Policy
motion_text:
AMENDMENT MOVED by Councillor Maloney
SECONDED by Councillor Orr

A. THAT Council adopt the Coastal Flood Management Policy, generally as
presented in Appendix A to the Report dated March 17, 2026, entitled “Coastal
Flood Management Policy.”

B. THAT Council directs staff to report back on the scope of work, governance
options, resource requirements, and timeline necessary for the City to take the
steps necessary to convene, or cause to be convened, an intergovernmental and
inter-agency task force for the False Creek floodplain, for the purpose of:

1. identifying major publicly owned, utility, transportation, health, and civic
assets at risk from coastal flooding and sea level rise;

2. assessing whether a coordinated, area-wide structural flood management
approach would be more effective and cost-efficient than fragmented site-
by-site measures;

3. identifying the appropriate roles of the City, Province, Government of
Canada, First Nations, agencies, utilities, and other major landowners
and infrastructure owners, including, but not limited to, Canada Mortgage
and Housing Corporation in respect of Granville Island, the Department of
National Defence and/or the Canadian Coast Guard in respect of the
Kitsilano Coast Guard Station, Fisheries and Oceans Canada in respect
of the False Creek Harbour Authority, PAVCo in respect of B.C. Place,
Providence Health Care in respect to St. Paul's Hospital, Vancouver
Fraser Port Authority, Vancouver Airport Authority, TransLink, BC Hydro,
Creative Energy, and such other affected public or regulated entities as
staff may determine;

4. identifying advocacy, research, technical, and partnership work required
to support any future funding strategy or senior-government engagement;
and

5. reporting back on options for a fiscally prudent convening and
coordination role for the City that does not prejudice future Council
decisions on capital commitments.

C. THAT the report back in B above also assesses whether similar
multi-jurisdictional coordination challenges exist in the Burrard Inlet and Fraser
River floodplains, or whether differences in land ownership, infrastructure
ownership, and distribution of benefits mean that a False Creek-specific
approach is warranted.
summary: Proposes adopting coastal flood policy and studying an intergovernmental task force and coordinated flood-management options for False Creek and other floodplains.
rationale: The exact minutes excerpt provides the proposed policy adoption and detailed report-back instructions.

motion_group_title: Motion 3. Cheap, Easy and Everywhere: Unlocking the full potential of shared mobility to reduce
motion_text:
AMENDMENT MOVED by Councillor Klassen
SECONDED by Councillor Kirby-Yung
THAT A and B be deleted and substituted with the following:
THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED THAT Council affirm its support for bike-
sharing as an essential component of a comprehensive and well-integrated
regional transportation and mobility system, and request that the Mayor write to

Standing Committee of Council on City Finance and Services
Minutes, Wednesday, March 11, 2026 13
TransLink, with copies to the Mayors’ Council on Regional Transportation and
the BC Minister of Transportation and Transit, advocating that TransLink explore
opportunities to develop and deliver an integrated regional bike-share system to
improve first- and last-mile connections to transit and expand affordable mobility
options across Metro Vancouver;
FURTHER THAT Council’s advocacy highlight potential opportunities for regional
coordination, including integration with the regional transit system, fare or pass
integration, coordinated planning of shared mobility networks, and equitable
access across municipalities in the region.

FINAL MOTION AS APPROVED
WHEREAS
1. Shared active-transportation services, including bike-share systems, contribute to
cleaner air, improved public health outcomes, quieter neighbourhoods, and
reduced traffic congestion, while providing residents with efficient and affordable
mobility options (Urban Mobility, 2025);
2. In 2020, the City of Vancouver established a goal to ensure that two-thirds of all
in-city trips would be made by active transportation and transit modes by 2030
(City of Vancouver, 2020);
3. With an initial $5 million investment from the City, in 2016 Vancouver Bike Share
Inc. launched the Mobi (by Rogers) system. The company now services 264 bike
share stations and 2,600 bikes, including 600 e-bikes;
4. Vancouver Bike Share Inc. now self-finances its operations via advertising and
user fees, while also compensating the City for its use of parking spaces for
docking stations;
5. A growing number of people are using Mobi (by Rogers), however the unequal
distribution of stations across the city, and its limited intermodal and inter-regional
connections are likely limiting its potential (Vancouver Sun, 2025);
6. Vancouver’s bike share system trails those of both Toronto and Montreal in both
system size and affordability. Compared with Vancouver, Montreal’s system
offers nearly twice as many shared bikes per resident (Vancouver Sun, 2025);
7. The cities of Montreal and Toronto formally recognize the public benefit of bike-
share systems and invest in them accordingly, whereas Vancouver's now
operates on a cost-recovery basis;

Standing Committee of Council on City Finance and Services
Minutes, Wednesday, March 11, 2026 14
8. An opportunity exists for the City to collaborate with other Metro Vancouver local
governments on a safe, sustainable, and convenient regional bike-share network
that would bring broad public benefits including reduced traffic congestion;
9. Studies show that cities can significantly boost bike-share uptake, especially
among low-income residents, by increasing station coverage in underserved
areas, lowering prices, and improving accessibility via, for example, a unified
pass that would work across all public transit modes (Transportation Research
Record, 2025);
10. Given the strong evidence base for their societal benefits, bike-share systems
deserve recognition as a legitimate mode of public transportation; and
11. Directing public investments to a regional bike-share system would provide
significant and measurable returns for Metro Vancouver residents (Urban
Mobility, 2025).
THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED THAT Council affirm its support for bike-sharing as an
essential component of a comprehensive and well-integrated regional transportation and
mobility system, and request that the Mayor write to TransLink, with copies to the
Mayors’ Council on Regional Transportation and the BC Minister of Transportation and
Transit, advocating that TransLink explore opportunities to develop and deliver an
integrated regional bike-share system to improve first- and last-mile connections to
transit and expand affordable mobility options across Metro Vancouver;
FURTHER THAT Council’s advocacy highlight potential opportunities for regional
coordination, including integration with the regional transit system, fare or pass
integration, coordinated planning of shared mobility networks, and equitable access
across municipalities in the region.
The Committee adjourned at 12:10 pm.

agenda_description: Motion 2. Advancing the Right to Food and Public Food Infrastructure
motion_group_title: Motion 2. Advancing the Right to Food and Public Food Infrastructure
motion_text:
MOVED by Councillor Orr
SECONDED by Councillor Maloney
THAT the Committee recommend to Council
WHEREAS
1. Access to nutritious, affordable, and culturally appropriate food is a human right
and a core social determinant of health;
2. In January 2013, Council adopted the Vancouver Food Strategy, committing the
City to support food friendly neighbourhoods, improve access to healthy and
culturally diverse food, strengthen a green food economy, and advocate for a just
and sustainable food system, recognizing that food is essential for strong and
connected communities;
3. Thirteen years later, significant inequities persist, and food access remains
unevenly distributed;
4. The BC Centre for Disease Control has identified household food insecurity as a
serious public health issue rooted in systemic inequities, and food access

Standing Committee of Council on City Finance and Services
Minutes, Wednesday, March 11, 2026 10
remains unevenly distributed across Vancouver, with lower income
neighbourhoods facing the greatest barriers;
5. The City’s Equitable Access to Healthy Food Retail Report identified Food
Priority Zones, primarily in the Downtown Eastside and southeast Vancouver,
where residents have limited access to full-service grocery stores and higher
rates of food insecurity;
6. The Downtown Eastside is home to the largest Urban Indigenous population in
British Columbia, as well as the highest concentration of seniors and people with
disabilities in Vancouver, yet continues to lack equitable access to dignified food
retail;
7. The potential loss of long-standing neighbourhood food assets highlights the
fragility of culturally significant and affordable food infrastructure, particularly for
Chinese, Japanese, and other communities that rely on culturally appropriate
foods;
8. Four corporations control the majority of Canada’s grocery market, limiting
competition and contributing to rising food costs that disproportionately impact
low-income residents; and
9. While income supports remain the jurisdiction of senior governments, the City of
Vancouver has tools within its authority, including publicly owned land, zoning
powers, and leases, to strengthen equitable and community-based food
infrastructure.
THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED
A. THAT Council affirm the human right to adequate, nutritious, safe, and culturally
appropriate food as a guiding principle in City planning, land use, economic, and
social policy decisions.
B. THAT Council direct staff to report back with the following:
(i) A list of City owned land and commercial spaces in Food Priority Zones,
beginning with the Downtown Eastside;
(ii) Policy options to pilot at least one publicly owned or community operated
grocery store on City land; and
(iii) Tools to stabilize and protect culturally significant and affordable food
retail.
summary: Proposed affirming a right to adequate food and requesting options for community grocery infrastructure and protection of affordable food retailers.
rationale: The exact minutes excerpt clearly states the proposed principle and requested staff report.

motion_group_title: Motion 1. A One-Time Extraordinary Grant for Granville Street Activation During FIFA World Cup
motion_text:
FINAL MOTION AS APPROVED
WHEREAS
1. The City of Vancouver will soon host seven FIFA World Cup 2026 matches at BC
Place, welcoming more than 50,000 ticketed spectators per match and
generating significant additional visitor activity throughout the downtown core;
2. Downtown Vancouver will fall within the required 2-kilometre FIFA “Controlled
Area” on each match day and the day prior, requiring coordinated planning to
support safety, emergency access, and regulated commercial activity;
3. Granville Street between West Georgia Street and Davie Street is proposed to be
temporarily pedestrianized from June 11 to July 19, 2026 (39 consecutive days)
to enhance pedestrian safety, support local businesses, and create a welcoming
public gathering space during the tournament period;
4. The Downtown Vancouver Business Improvement Association, representing
approximately 8,000 businesses and property owners across 90 blocks of the
downtown core, has committed to leading marketing, placemaking, beautification,
micro-cleaning, and street-level activation initiatives along Granville Street during
this period;
5. The City of Vancouver will be responsible for core operational requirements
including transit re-routing, street closures, policing, security, sanitation, and
general stewardship, while the Downtown Vancouver BIA will assume

Standing Committee of Council on City Finance and Services
Minutes, Wednesday, March 11, 2026 7
responsibility for activation programming and related enhancements;
6. FIFA security requirements and limited policing resources restrict large-scale
stage concerts or public viewing installations on Granville Street, necessitating a
pedestrian-focused activation model emphasizing expanded patios, small-scale
performances such as buskers, interactive and “Instagramable” installations,
beautification, and enhancements to the public realm that are playful,
approachable, accessible, and suitable for all ages;
7. A sustained, free, and inclusive activation will ensure that residents and visitors,
including those without match tickets, can participate in the energy and
excitement of the tournament and support downtown businesses under the
theme “Make Downtown Your Goal”;
8. The Downtown Vancouver BIA is the largest Business Improvement Association
in Western Canada and has demonstrated expertise and capacity in delivering
economic development initiatives and public realm programming at scale;
9. Council has replenished the City’s financial reserves over the past several years
and may allocate one-time funding for strategic, time-limited initiatives that
advance economic vitality, enhance public safety and vibrancy, and showcase
Vancouver positively to a global audience; and
11. A one-time extraordinary grant of $300,000 represents a modest and strategic
investment to complement the $800,000 financial contribution by Downtown
Vancouver BIA to support programming on Granville St FIFA World Cup 2026,
help offset the BIA’s financial burden and elevate the Granville Street activation
from good to great during a once-in-a-generation international event.
THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED
A. THAT Council approve a one-time extraordinary grant of up to $300,000 to the
Downtown Vancouver Business Improvement Association, funded from the City’s
available financial reserves, to complement the BIA’s significant financial
contribution and offset eligible costs associated with activation, placemaking,
beautification, marketing, micro-cleaning, and enhanced stewardship of Granville
Street between West Georgia Street and Davie Street during the FIFA World Cup
2026 period (June 11 to July 19, 2026).
B. THAT Council direct the General Manager of Engineering Services in
collaboration with the FWC26 Chief Delivery Officer to work with the Downtown
Vancouver Business Improvement Association and enter into a funding
agreement outlining eligible expenditures, reporting requirements, and
compliance with applicable City policies and FIFA-related regulations.
C. THAT Council direct City staff to work with the Downtown BIA to arrange for any
permits required to enable a Downtown Vancouver Business Improvement
Association-led activation initiative taking place during the period in which
Vancouver is hosting 2026 FIFA World Cup matches, supported in part by a City

Standing Committee of Council on City Finance and Services
Minutes, Wednesday, March 11, 2026 8
of Vancouver grant on the five blocks of Granville Street identified in this motion
(West Georgia Street to Davie Street) and, if it is determined that any by-law
amendments are needed in order to facilitate the activation initiative, that Council
direct the Director of Legal Services to prepare those amendments and bring
them forward for enactment by Council.
D. THAT Council direct staff to report back to Council following the conclusion of the
activation period with a summary of outcomes, including activation results,
business participation, and opportunities for legacy reuse of installations and
public realm improvements.
E. THAT Council delegate its authority to execute the grant agreement for the
associated amount that includes terms and conditions that are consistent with the
intentions of this motion, that satisfy the City’s Director of Legal Services, and
that disburse the grant described in this motion to the City Manager (or their
designate).
F. THAT no legal rights or obligations will arise or be created by Council’s adoption
of the clauses above unless and until all legal documentation has been executed
and delivered by the respective parties).

agenda_description: Urgent Action to Save Car Free Days 2026 - FINAL MOTION AS AMENDED
motion_group_title: Urgent Action to Save Car Free Days 2026
motion_text:
FINAL MOTION AS APPROVED
WHEREAS
1. Free and accessible public events play an important role in building community
connection and civic pride, especially at a time when many residents are facing
cost-of-living pressures and fewer opportunities to enjoy shared cultural
experiences without financial barriers;
2. For more than 15 years, Car Free Days have been among Vancouver’s largest
and most recognizable public events, attracting substantial local participation and
visitors, and contributing to the city’s cultural life, tourism, and economic activity
(Car Free Vancouver Society);
3. The Car Free Days have historically attracted tens of thousands attendees
annually, including a significant proportion of out-of-City of Vancouver visitors,
and generated measurable community and economic benefits for the city
(Destination Vancouver, 2025);
4. The Car Free Days mobilize hundreds of volunteers, strengthen community
bonds and neighbourhood cohesion; and provide a platform for local artists,
artisans and businesses to showcase their work (Vancouver Sun, 2026);
5. On March 2, 2026, the Vancouver Car Free Day Society announced the
cancellation of Car Free Days for summer 2026 after rising production and
operating costs, combined with insufficient City funding or other support, made
the multi-day event financially unsustainable;
6. Through the FestShare program, the City of Vancouver committed to providing a
fee reduction of up to $75,000 to partially offset municipal service costs for the
event, including policing, fire and emergency coordination, engineering, traffic
operations, sanitation, waste management, park access, and post-event cleanup;
notwithstanding such fee reduction, event organizers remain liable for a
substantial balance of municipal service fees at the conclusion of the festival.
(Vancouver Sun, 2026);
7. The City’s Arts, Culture and Community Services department offers a range of
programs, awards and services to support cultural projects but has been subject
to a 12% budget reduction for 2026;

Council Meeting
Minutes, March 10, 2026 27

8. Following the cancellation announcement, Vancouver residents publicly
expressed disappointment that a $30,000 funding gap led to the cancellation of
the Car Free Days;
9. Bridging this $30,000 funding gap reaffirms the City’s commitment to vibrant
public events and to ensuring Vancouverites have access to free and affordable
events such as Car Free Days; and
10. Without the Car Free Day series, there is a noticeable gap in Vancouver’s
summer events calendar, particularly in the period following FIFA 2026, when the
city is expected to continue welcoming elevated numbers of visitors and
international attention.
THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED

A. THAT Council approve the allocation of a one-time grant of up to $30,000 from
appropriate City reserves, contingency funds, or other available sources to
support the delivery of the 2026 Car Free Days series.

B. THAT the funding of $30,000 is conditional upon the event organizers providing
the City with a financial and event delivery plan satisfactory to staff,
demonstrating how the requested funding will address the identified shortfall and
enable the events to proceed, specifically the Commercial Drive Car Free Day
event on September 5, 2026, and the Main Street Car Free Day event on
September 13, 2026.

C. THAT staff report back to Council no later than March 31, 2026, with:

i) details of funding source identification; and
ii) an event delivery plan prior to distributing funds to the Car Free Day
society on or before April 15, 2026, in accordance with City’s financial
policies and grant administration practices.

D. THAT any cash funding associated with the motion entitled “Urgent Action to
Save Car Free Days 2026”, is a grant and that Council delegate its authority to
execute any grant agreement for the associated amount that includes terms and
conditions that are consistent with the intentions of the above-noted motion, that
satisfy the City’s Director of Legal Services, and that disburse the grant
described in the same motion to the City Manager (or their designate).

E. THAT no legal rights or obligations will arise or be created by Council’s adoption
of A to D above unless and until all legal documentation has been executed and
delivered by the respective parties).

ENQUIRIES AND OTHER MATTERS

None.

Council Meeting
Minutes, March 10, 2026 28

ADJOURNMENT

MOVED by Councillor Kirby-Yung
SECONDED by Councillor Montague

THAT the meeting be adjourned.

CARRIED UNANIMOUSLY

Council adjourned at 4:33 pm.

* * * * *
summary: Approved a conditional one-time grant of up to $30,000 to support two 2026 Car Free Day events.
rationale: The exact minutes excerpt clearly states the grant, conditions, events, and reporting requirements.

motion_group_title: 2026 Property Tax: Development Potential Relief and Land Assessment Averaging
motion_text:
MOVED by Councillor Dominato
SECONDED by Councillor Klassen

Development Potential Relief

A. THAT Council approve, in principle, the extension of the pilot development
potential relief program (“Pilot DPRP”) in 2026 for eligible Light Industry (Class 5)
and Business and Other (Class 6) properties with the following parameters:

a. the additional City eligibility criteria and exclusions established by the
Development Potential Tax Relief Declaration By-law, 2026 (No. 14520);
b. the percentage of assessed land value by neighborhood/zoning district up
to a maximum of $6.5 million for each eligible property, as outlined in
Appendix A of the Report dated February 23, 2026, entitled “2026
Property Tax: Development Potential Relief and Land Assessment
Averaging”;
c. that the eligible land value be taxed at a general purpose tax rate that is
50% lower than the blended rate for Classes 5 and 6;
FURTHER THAT the Director of Legal Services, in consultation with the Director
of Finance, be instructed to bring forward for enactment a by-law in accordance
with this decision.

Council Meeting
Minutes, March 10, 2026 15

Land Assessment Averaging

B. THAT Council approve, in principle, the continuation of targeted 5-year land
assessment averaging (“Targeted Averaging”) in 2026 for Residential (Class 1),
Light Industry (Class 5), and Business and Other (Class 6) properties with the
following parameters, generally consistent with those of the 2025 Land
Assessment Averaging By-law (No. 14293):
a. a threshold of 10% above the class average change for Class 1 and for
Classes 5 and 6 (finalized using the 2026 Revised Assessment Roll) to
define eligibility;
b. that applying the averaging formula to eligible properties will not result in:
i. a change in assessment falling below the “threshold”; or;
ii. a reduction in values exceeding $6.5 million;
c. general exclusions for unimproved properties, new entries to the
assessment roll, subdivided or consolidated properties, property class
changes, and changes in the status of a property under section 19(8) of
the Assessment Act;
d. rezoning related exclusions for properties subject of:
i. a policy statement approved during the last two years;
ii. a proposed rezoning approved in principle during the last two
years, or;
iii. a rezoning enacted during the last year;
except for those initiated by the Director of Planning and rezonings to
certain townhouse district schedules which will still be considered for
Targeted Averaging;
e. an exclusion for properties that receive relief under the 2026 Pilot DPRP;
FURTHER THAT the Director of Legal Services, in consultation with the Director of
Finance, be instructed to bring forward for enactment a by-law in accordance with this
decision.

agenda_description: M6. Honouring the Horse: Saving Vancouver's Iconic Lunar New Year Community Gala in Chinatown
motion_group_title: M6. Honouring the Horse: Saving Vancouver's Iconic Lunar New Year Community Gala in Chinatown
motion_text:
FINAL MOTION AS APPROVED

WHEREAS

1. Lunar New Year celebrations are an important cultural, economic, and
community-building tradition in Vancouver, particularly for the city’s Chinese and
broader Asian communities, and contribute significantly to Vancouver’s cultural
vibrancy, tourism economy, and downtown vitality;

2. The Chinese Benevolent Association (CBA) has a long-standing role in
organizing and hosting the annual Lunar New Year Gala, which is widely
regarded as a signature cultural event with deep historical roots in Chinatown
and regional and international significance;

3. The Lunar New Year Gala has historically been hosted at the Floata Restaurant
banquet venue space in Chinatown, a location with strong cultural resonance,
symbolic importance, and accessibility for the community;

4. The recent closure of Floata Restaurant has created unexpected and immediate
financial, operational, and logistical challenges for the CBA in hosting the 2026
Lunar New Year Gala in the same venue space, pending the identification of a
long-term restaurant tenant or permanent venue solution;

5. Without short-term, one-time financial and operational support, there is a risk that
the 2026 Lunar New Year Gala may be cancelled or significantly scaled back,
resulting in cultural, economic, and reputational impacts to Chinatown and the
City more broadly;

6. Providing temporary, targeted support represents a time-limited measure to
ensure continuity of a signature community cultural event while longer-term
venue solutions are explored; and

7. On November 17, 2025, the Chinatown Advisory Committee unanimously passed
a motion requesting that Mayor and Council direct staff to explore one-time
funding opportunities to support the Chinese Benevolent Association’s 2026
Spring Festival Gala, particularly in light of the closure of Floata Restaurant.

THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED

A. THAT Council approve a one-time extraordinary grant of up to $60,000 from the
City’s 2026 Operating Budget, or another funding source deemed appropriate by
the General Manager of Finance, to the Chinese Benevolent Association (CBA)
to assist with costs associated with hosting the 2026 Lunar New Year Gala at the
former Floata Restaurant banquet venue space;

Standing Committee of Council on City Finance and Services
Minutes, Wednesday, February 4, 2026 21

FURTHER THAT it be noted explicitly that this grant support is extraordinary and
one-time in nature, intended solely to address the unique circumstances arising
from the closure of Floata Restaurant and not as ongoing event funding.

B. THAT Council approve a license of the 4th floor of Chinatown Plaza from
February 21 through February 24, 2026, at a nominal rate ($10) which
constitutes an in-kind grant of $4,490;

FURTHER THAT it be noted explicitly that this in-kind grant support is
extraordinary and one-time in nature.

C. THAT Council delegate its authority to execute the grant agreement that includes
terms and conditions that are consistent with the intentions of this motion, that
satisfy the City’s Director of Legal Services, and that disburse the grants
described in this report to the City’s Deputy City Manager (or their designate).

D. THAT Council direct City staff to expedite all necessary City permitting processes
required for the 2026 Lunar New Year Gala, recognizing the tight planning and
delivery timelines for the event.

E. THAT Council direct City staff to work collaboratively with Vancouver Coastal
Health to assist in expediting any required health approvals or permits necessary
for the successful and timely delivery of the event.
The Committee adjourned at 3:25 pm.

agenda_description: M5. Bus To Move: Prioritizing Transit Trouble Spots for Snow and Ice Removal
motion_group_title: M5. Bus To Move: Prioritizing Transit Trouble Spots for Snow and Ice Removal
motion_text:
MOVED by Councillor Maloney
SECONDED by Councillor Orr

THAT the Committee recommend to Council

WHEREAS

1. The City of Vancouver Snow and Ice Treatment Policy (2021) governs the
prioritization of snow removal operations on City-owned road infrastructure;

2. The Policy accords the highest priority to First Priority Locations and calls for
these locations to be treated within 12 hours from the end of a snowfall event;

3. First Priority Locations include bus routes, but also several broad additional
categories of roadways in the city, namely major roads, emergency access
routes, bridges and viaducts, school routes, and key pedestrian pathways;

4. This category is so broad as to be indiscriminate and fails to internally prioritize
known problematic spots for buses ahead of the hundreds of other First Priority
Locations. For instance, the category of ‘major roads’ includes virtually every
roadway on the Downtown Peninsula;
5. As a result, despite being classified as First Priority Locations, known problem
areas on bus routes often experience significant delays in snow clearance,
despite buses on corridors with slopes being at greater risk of losing traction than
private vehicles;

6. Even a slight delay to snow clearing on an inclined bus route can affect not only
the tens of thousands of riders on that route but also many others, as schedules
are often linked;

7. Prioritizing a small set of corridors that cause problems for bus traction can yield
major reliability gains throughout the entire city;

8. According to the 2024 Transportation Survey, 9% of all trips in the City of
Vancouver are made by bus, accounting for an estimated 144,000 trips each
day;

9. Essential workers who rely on cars or bicycles are unlikely to have snow tires in
our region, and they should have a reliable alternative to using their vehicle in
potentially unsafe conditions;

10. Maintaining the reliability of transit in winter conditions is possible and is crucial
for our healthcare system and our economy.

THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED THAT Council direct staff to consult with Coast
Mountain Bus Company (CMBC) to identify and prioritize known problem areas where
the delayed removal of snow and ice has caused operational problems for transit buses
in the past;

Standing Committee of Council on City Finance and Services
Minutes, Wednesday, February 4, 2026 18

FURTHER THAT Council direct staff to take immediate steps to prioritize transit
reliability during snow events, especially in places where bus service has been disrupted
in recent years;

AND FURTHER THAT Council direct staff to study, consult with CMBC, and report back
with proposed revisions to the City of Vancouver Snow and Ice Treatment Policy to
prioritize the immediate and consistent clearing of snow and ice from known problem
areas for transit buses in future years.
summary: Directs consultation, immediate snow-clearing prioritization for transit trouble spots, and study of future policy revisions.
rationale: The exact minutes excerpt clearly specifies operational prioritization alongside consultation and study.

agenda_description: M4. Advancing Democratic Innovation in Vancouver Municipal Elections to Increase Voter Turnout and Improve Democratic Legitimacy
motion_group_title: M4. Advancing Democratic Innovation in Vancouver Municipal Elections to Increase Voter Turnout and Improve Democratic Legitimacy
motion_text:
MOVED by Councillor Orr
SECONDED by Councillor Fry

THAT the Committee recommend to Council

WHEREAS

Standing Committee of Council on City Finance and Services
Minutes, Wednesday, February 4, 2026 15

1. Vancouver’s municipal democracy depends on broad, equitable, and meaningful
participation by residents. Yet persistent structural, logistical, and institutional
barriers limit access to voting and weaken democratic legitimacy;

2. Addressing declining turnout, improving access to the vote, and ensuring that the
results of elections reflect the will of a majority of voters are essential to
maintaining public trust and strengthening civic engagement;

3. Voter turnout in Vancouver municipal elections has been decreasing in each
general election since 2014. In 2022, the election saw only a 36% turnout. The
2025 by-election saw record turnout for a by-election despite only 15.09% of
voters casting their ballots;

4. Vancouver has set a target to increase municipal voter turnout to at least 60% by
2025 in the Healthy City Strategy (2014-2025);

5. Lack of transportation can be a barrier for voters to make it to the polls. Many
transit agencies in North America have offered fare-free transit on election days
as a way to reduce obstacles and encourage voting (for example, 10 of the
largest U.S. transit systems made rides free on Election Day 2020.) Making
transit free on Election Day can remove an obstacle and improve access to
democracy;

6. Another method of increasing voter access is mobile polling stations. The City of
Calgary’s “Vote Bus” program, first introduced in 2013, is a mobile polling station
on a transit bus that travels to multiple spots during the advance voting period. In
the 2025 Calgary municipal election, for example, the Vote Bus visited 11
different locations across the city, enabling more residents to easily vote in
advance polls;

7. Vancouver’s Mayor is currently elected by a first-past-the-post (plurality) vote,
which in multi-candidate races can result in a winner who lacks majority support.
Mayors in B.C. municipalities have been elected with well under 40% of the vote
(for example, Surrey’s 2022 mayor won with just 28.14%) raising concerns about
inadequate democratic representation and voter expression

8. Ranked choice voting (RCV) is used by every major federal political party in
Canada for leadership elections, and over 40 local jurisdictions across the United
States including New York, NY and San Francisco, CA. Exit polls consistently
show that a majority of voters who experience RCV want to keep it. For example,
77% of New York City voters wanted to keep RCV after its first use in 2021.
Evidence shows that people in cities with preferential voting were less likely to
view campaigns as negative, and less likely to say that candidates were
frequently criticizing each other;

9. There’s evidence to show that Ranked Choice Voting (RCV) boosts voter turnout.
In 2021 in New York, turnout increased by 36% over the previous open-seat
mayoral race. In the 2018 mayoral election in San Francisco, more voters
participated in the ranked-choice vote for Mayor than the non-ranked races for
Governor and US Senator; and

Standing Committee of Council on City Finance and Services
Minutes, Wednesday, February 4, 2026 16

10. The City of Vancouver must take all appropriate steps to engage the public in
democratic processes, work to reverse the trend of declining voter turnout, and
take concrete steps to reach the bold 60% turnout goal set by City Council in the
Healthy City Strategy.

THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED

A. THAT Council directs staff to write a letter to TransLink to establish a plan for
a mobile “Vote Bus” polling station in the 2026 election, modelled after
Calgary’s “Vote Bus”, with a report back to Council with options for
approval (including estimated costs to the City of Vancouver) by Q2 2026.

B. THAT Council directs staff to write a letter to TransLink to develop a plan for a
modestly scaled fare-free transit pilot on general voting day and advance
voting days for the 2026 City Election, to report back by Q2 of 2026 to
Council for review and approval, including estimated costs to the City of
Vancouver, considering the following options:

• Existing routes with high potential for increasing turnout on advance
voting days and on general voting day;

• Possible shuttle routes outside the regular TransLink network that could
have a high per-dollar impact for populations which are less likely to vote.

C. THAT Council directs staff to prepare a report (due Q1 2027) on making transit
fare-free on general election day in 2030, including considerations on:

• Making all transit fare-free on General Election Day;

• Targeted routes for advanced voting days;

• Shuttle routes outside the regular TransLink network that could have a
high per-dollar impact for populations which are less likely to vote.

D. THAT Council directs staff to prepare a report (due Q1 2027) on implementing a
ranked-choice ballot for the 2030 mayoral election, including legal requirements
and technical considerations, and outlining multiple options for Council’s
consideration based on other municipal jurisdictions.
summary: Proposes plans and reports on mobile polling, election-day transit access, and ranked-choice voting for future municipal elections.
rationale: The exact minutes excerpt details the requested election-access plans and reports.

a letter to the Province of British Columbia requesting that general admission to the PNE
Amphitheatre be made free of charge for the public during FIFA World Cup 2026
match−day live screenings, to ensure families, youth, and residents of all incomes can
participate in and enjoy the tournament through accessible community viewing events.

2. Igniting our Spirits: Bringing Vancouver Together Through Summer Celebration

* * * * *

During discussion, it was

MOVED by Councillor Meiszner
SECONDED by Councillor Dominato

THAT, as per section 2.8(a) of the Procedure By-law, Council extend the meeting past
noon in order to complete Motion 2.

CARRIED UNANIMOUSLY AND
BY THE REQUIRED MAJORITY

* * * * *
MOVED by Mayor Sim
SECONDED by Councillor Kirby-Yung

THAT the Committee recommend to Council

WHEREAS

1. Free and accessible public events play an important role in building community
connection and civic pride, especially at a time when many residents are facing
cost-of-living pressures and fewer opportunities to enjoy shared cultural
experiences without financial barriers;

2. The Celebration of Light (formerly the Symphony of Fire) has for more than three
decades been one of Vancouver’s largest and most recognizable public events,

Standing Committee of Council on City Finance and Services
Minutes, Wednesday, February 4, 2026 10

attracting substantial local attendance and significant visitor participation, and
contributing to the city’s cultural, tourism, and economic activity;

3. In November 2025, the Vancouver Fireworks Festival Society announced the
indefinite cancellation of the Celebration of Light after rising production and
operating costs, combined with the loss of federal funding, reduced provincial
support, and declining private sponsorship, made the multi-night event financially
unsustainable;

4. Federal funding for the event declined from approximately $450,000 in 2023 to
zero by 2025–26, while provincial funding remained unchanged for more than a
decade and was proposed for reduction, significantly reducing the real value of
senior-government support;

5. Despite these funding challenges, the City of Vancouver had indicated its
intention to continue providing in-kind municipal services required for the event,
including policing, fire and emergency coordination, engineering, traffic
operations, sanitation, waste management, park access, and post-event cleanup,
with an estimated annual value of $1.2 million to $1.6 million, pursuant to Council
direction established in 2001;

6. The Celebration of Light historically attracted approximately 1.3 million attendees
annually, including a significant proportion of out-of-region visitors, and
generated measurable tourism and economic benefits for the city and region;

7. Following the cancellation announcement, the Mayor of Vancouver publicly
expressed disappointment over reductions in senior-government funding and
affirmed the City’s willingness to explore ways to ensure Vancouverites can
continue to enjoy a major summer fireworks celebration;

8. The reinstatement of a multi-night international fireworks competition would
require long-term funding commitments from federal and provincial governments
and private partners beyond the City’s sole capacity; and

9. Without the Celebration of Light, there is a noticeable gap in Vancouver’s
summer events calendar, particularly in the period following FIFA 2026, when the
city is expected to continue welcoming elevated numbers of visitors and
international attention.

THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED

A. THAT Council request the Mayor write a letter to the Government of Canada and
the Province of British Columbia urging the reinstatement and increase of federal
and provincial funding necessary to enable the return and long-term viability of
the Celebration of Light, recognizing the event’s longstanding cultural
significance, its contribution to tourism and the local economy, and its importance
as a free public experience for residents and visitors.

motion_text:
AMENDMENT MOVED by Councillor Fry
SECONDED by Councillor Orr

THAT the following be added as a new letter:

THAT the proposed CD-1 By-law be amended to include a new definition as
follows:

“Below-Market Rental Units” means dwelling units where the maximum
starting rents are set at least 20% less than the average rents for all
private rental apartment units city-wide, as published by the Canada
Mortgage and Housing Corporation in the Rental Market Report, all as
secured by a housing agreement registered on title to the property.

FURTHER THAT the Conditions of Use in the proposed CD-1 By-law be
amended to include a new condition as follows:

Conditions of Use

A minimum of 20% of the total dwelling area must be below-market rental
units.

AND FURTHER THAT the Conditions of By-law Enactment be amended
by adding as a new 2.6:

Part 2 Conditions – Housing

2.6 Make arrangements to the satisfaction of the General Manager of
Planning, Urban Design and Sustainability and the Director of Legal
Services to enter into a Housing Agreement and a Section 219 Covenant
to secure all residential units as class A for profit affordable rental
housing, excluding Seniors Supportive or Independent Living Housing,
and including at least 20% of the residential floor area that is counted in
the calculation of the dwelling unit area per the CD-1 By-law to be
secured as below-market rental dwelling housing units, and the remaining

Public Hearing
Minutes, February 3 and 10, 2026 11

units to be secured as market rental units, subject to the conditions set
out below for such units, subject to the conditions set out below for such
units, for a term equal to the longer of 60 years and the life of the building
and such other terms and conditions as the General Manager of
Planning, Urban Design and Sustainability and the Director of Legal
Services may require. The agreement or agreements will include but not
be limited to the following terms and conditions:

(a) A no separate-sales covenant;

(b) A no stratification covenant;

(c) A provision that none of the units will be rented for less than 90
consecutive days at a time;

(d) That the average initial starting monthly rents by unit type for the
below-market rental housing dwelling units in the project will be at
least 20% below the average market rent for private rental
apartment units city-wide as published by the most recent Canada
Mortgage and Housing Corporation in the Rental Market Survey
Data Tables for Vancouver at the time when the Occupancy
Permit is issued;

(e) That a rent roll indicating the agreed maximum average initial
monthly rents for the below-market rental housing dwelling units
will be required prior issuance of an Occupancy Permit, to the
satisfaction of the General Manager of Planning, Urban Design or
Sustainability (or successor in function) and the Director of Legal
Services;

(f) Following initial occupancy, on a change in tenancy for a below-
market rental housing dwelling unit, the starting rent for such new
tenancy will be at least 20% below the rent for private rental
apartment units city-wide as published by the Canada Mortgage
and Housing Corporation in the most recent Rental Market Survey
Data Tables for Vancouver for that unit type at the time of the
change in tenancy;

(g) That the applicant will verify eligibility of new tenants for the
below-market rental housing dwelling units, based on the
following:

(i) For new tenants, annual household income cannot exceed
(4) four times the annual rent for the unit (i.e. at least 25%
of household income is spent on rent); and

(ii) There should be at least one occupant per bedroom in the
unit.

Public Hearing
Minutes, February 3 and 10, 2026 12

(h) That the applicant will verify the ongoing eligibility of existing
tenants in below-market rental housing dwelling units every five
(5) years after initial occupancy:

(i) For such tenants, annual household income cannot
exceed 5 times the annual rent for the unit (i.e. at least
20% of income is spent on rent); and

(ii) There should be at least one occupant per bedroom in the
unit.

(i) On an annual basis, or at the request of the City, the applicant will
report to the City of Vancouver on the operation of the below-
market rental housing dwelling units which will ensure that the City
can confirm that the units are being operated as agreed, and will
include a rent roll for the below-market rental housing dwelling
units, and a summary of the results of eligibility testing for these
units; and

(j) Such other terms and conditions as the General Manager of
Planning, Urban Design or Sustainability (or successor in function)
and the Director of Legal Services may require in their sole
discretion.

Note to Applicant: This condition will be secured by a Section 219 Covenant and a
Housing Agreement to be entered into by the City by the by-law enacted pursuant to
section 565.2 of the Vancouver Charter prior to enactment of the rezoning by-law.

agenda_description: Blinded by the Light: Improving Public Safety by Looking at Headlight Glare - Final Motion
motion_group_title: Blinded by the Light: Improving Public Safety by Looking at Headlight Glare - Final Motion
motion_text:
FINAL MOTION AS APPROVED

WHEREAS

1. Excessively bright vehicle headlights, including high-intensity discharge (HID)
and light-emitting diode (LED) headlights, are increasingly common on
Vancouver streets and are a growing source of glare for drivers, cyclists, and
pedestrians;

2. Headlight glare has been linked to reduced night-time visibility, delayed reaction
times, increased collision risk, and particular harm to seniors, people with
astigmatism or other vision impairments, cyclists, and pedestrians;

3. The proliferation of oversized vehicles with elevated headlight mounting heights,
combined with brighter factory-installed and aftermarket headlights, has
intensified glare impacts, especially on lower vehicles and active transportation
users;

4. Other jurisdictions have begun examining limits on headlight brightness, beam
pattern, mounting height, adaptive lighting behavior, and enforcement of illegal
aftermarket modifications; and

5. Vancouver has adopted Vision Zero goals and climate and transportation policies
that encourage walking, cycling, and transit, all of which are undermined when
street conditions feel unsafe due to vehicle glare.

THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED

A. THAT Council request that the Mayor write to the federal Minister of Transport
Canada urging continued and strengthened action to address excessive

Standing Committee of Council on Policy and Strategic Priorities
Minutes, Wednesday, January 21, 2026 14

headlight brightness and glare, including updates to national vehicle safety
standards and enforcement mechanisms, informed by safety impacts on drivers,
pedestrians, cyclists, seniors, and people with vision impairments.

B. THAT the following resolution entitled “Blinded by the Light: Improving Public
Safety by Looking at Headlight Glare” be submitted to the Federation of
Canadian Municipalities (FCM) for consideration at FCM's next Annual
Conference. Specifically, the resolution calls on the federal government to:

iv. establish clearer and enforceable limits on headlight brightness, beam
pattern, and mounting height;
v. strengthen oversight of adaptive and high-intensity lighting technologies;
and
vi. improve regulation and enforcement related to non-compliant aftermarket
vehicle lighting

-----------------------------------------------

Resolution - Blinded by the Light: Improving Public Safety by Looking at Headlight Glare

WHEREAS excessively bright vehicle headlights, including HID and LED headlights –
particularly when combined with oversized vehicles, elevated mounting heights, and illegal
aftermarket modifications – are increasingly common on Canadian roads and contribute to
significant glare that reduces night-time visibility, delays reaction times, and increases collision
risk, with disproportionate impacts on seniors, people with vision impairments, cyclists, and
pedestrians; and

WHEREAS Canada has adopted road safety, climate, and transportation policies that
encourage walking, cycling, and transit use, yet these objectives are undermined when street
conditions feel unsafe due to headlight glare, a concern that other jurisdictions have begun
addressing through limits on headlight brightness, beam patterns, mounting height, and
adaptive lighting behavior.

RESOLVED, That the Federation of Canadian Municipalities (FCM) call on the Federal
Government to take action to address excessive headlight brightness and glare, including
updates to national vehicle safety standards and enforcement mechanisms, informed by safety
impacts on drivers, pedestrians, cyclists, seniors, and people with vision impairments, with
specific actions to include:
iv. establish clearer and enforceable limits on headlight brightness, beam pattern,
and mounting height;
v. strengthen oversight of adaptive and high-intensity lighting technologies; and
vi. improve regulation and enforcement related to non-compliant aftermarket vehicle
lighting.

The Committee adjourned at 1:44 pm.

agenda_description: Blinded by the Light: Improving Public Safety by Looking at Headlight Glare - Amendment to B
motion_group_title: Blinded by the Light: Improving Public Safety by Looking at Headlight Glare
motion_text:
AMENDMENT MOVED by Councillor Kirby-Yung
SECONDED by Councillor Dominato

THAT B in the Motion be struck and the following inserted:

B. THAT the following resolution entitled “Blinded by the Light: Improving
Public Safety by Looking at Headlight Glare” be submitted to the
Federation of Canadian Municipalities (FCM) for consideration at FCM's
next Annual Conference. Specifically, the resolution calls on the federal
government to:

i. establish clearer and enforceable limits on headlight brightness,
beam pattern, and mounting height;
ii. strengthen oversight of adaptive and high-intensity lighting
technologies; and
iii. improve regulation and enforcement related to non-compliant
aftermarket vehicle lighting

-----------------------------------------------

Resolution - Blinded by the Light: Improving Public Safety by Looking at Headlight Glare

WHEREAS excessively bright vehicle headlights, including HID and LED headlights –
particularly when combined with oversized vehicles, elevated mounting heights, and illegal
aftermarket modifications – are increasingly common on Canadian roads and contribute to
significant glare that reduces night-time visibility, delays reaction times, and increases collision
risk, with disproportionate impacts on seniors, people with vision impairments, cyclists, and
pedestrians; and

WHEREAS Canada has adopted road safety, climate, and transportation policies that
encourage walking, cycling, and transit use, yet these objectives are undermined when street
conditions feel unsafe due to headlight glare, a concern that other jurisdictions have begun
addressing through limits on headlight brightness, beam patterns, mounting height, and
adaptive lighting behavior.

RESOLVED, That the Federation of Canadian Municipalities (FCM) call on the Federal
Government to take action to address excessive headlight brightness and glare, including
updates to national vehicle safety standards and enforcement mechanisms, informed by safety
impacts on drivers, pedestrians, cyclists, seniors, and people with vision impairments, with
specific actions to include:
i. establish clearer and enforceable limits on headlight brightness, beam pattern,
and mounting height;
ii. strengthen oversight of adaptive and high-intensity lighting technologies; and
iii. improve regulation and enforcement related to non-compliant aftermarket vehicle
lighting.
summary: Amends the motion to seek federal standards and enforcement addressing excessive vehicle-headlight brightness and glare.
rationale: The exact minutes excerpt specifies the requested federal regulatory and enforcement changes.

agenda_description: Paving the Way for More Non-Profit Housing in Vancouver
motion_group_title: Paving the Way for More Non-Profit Housing in Vancouver
motion_text:
organizations are key partners helping the City of Vancouver deliver stable non-
market housing;

2. Non-profit housing organizations are exempt from paying Development Cost
Levies (DCLs), and as a matter of Council policy, do not pay Community Amenity
Contributions (CACs) when they apply to rezone land (City of Vancouver, 2025).
The Vancouver Charter, section 523D(10)(d)(i) exempts social housing providers
from development charges;

3. The rising cost of construction and other economic pressures are making it more
difficult for for-profit residential developers to realise a financial return from
completed projects, thereby making it harder for them to commence the
construction of new projects. For-profit residential developers may welcome new
pathways to divest of completed or near-completed projects to non-profit housing
providers;

4. A recent example of this arose with the acquisition by BC Housing of a
completed building at 3077 Maddams Street from a for-profit developer. Once the
project was rezoned, Council was asked to approve a grant equivalent to the
development charges that would not have applied had BC Housing developed

Standing Committee of Council on Policy and Strategic Priorities
Minutes, Wednesday, January 21, 2026 9

the project directly, with a ⅔ majority vote required. The grant request was
initially denied, and Vancouver was at risk of losing out on the opportunity to
have 81 turn-key units of social housing for women and children before the
decision was reconsidered on December 9, 2025 (City of Vancouver, 2025);

5. It is advantageous to provide certainty of a DCL and CAC refund to non-profit
housing organizations that wish to purchase a building. Non-profit housing
providers do not have the flexibility to reduce their profit margin to cover delays
and unexpected costs. Certainty comes with a policy in place to provide a refund
at purchase, instead of the current model, which requires a request for a grant
that may not be approved;

6. The benefits of non-profit housing providers purchasing completed projects
include allowing them to provide social housing much more quickly, to the people
who need it, than if they had to develop a housing project from scratch. It gives
the non-profit housing providers more certainty for the end cost of the housing,
and results in housing that has been built to market standards;

7. There is currently no mechanism in the DCL By-Laws, where a completed project
is purchased by a non-profit housing organisation and rezoned for social
housing, to refund CACs or DCLs previously paid by the original for-profit
developer, once the deadline has passed for seeking a refund;

8. Currently, if a non-profit organisation purchases a completed building after the
deadline for refunding CACs and DCLs has passed, the new non-profit owner
needs to seek a grant from the City for an equivalent amount to the DCLs and
CACs they would have been exempt from paying if they had been the original
applicant, which is required to be voted on by a two-thirds majority of Council
members;

9. The existing process involves a great deal of uncertainty for non-profit housing
organizations, who must purchase the property, then apply for rezoning and only
then, apply to the City for a grant equivalent to a refund of the DCLs and CACs
they would have been exempt from paying if they had developed the project from
scratch, and have Council vote on it;

10. The 3077 Maddams Street purchase by BC Housing demonstrates the
complexity and uncertainty characterised by the existing system;

11. Providing non-profit housing providers with more certainty that they will be able to
recover the DCLs and CACs they would have been exempt from paying if they
had developed the building from scratch would provide an incentive for non-profit
housing providers to purchase recently completed buildings from for-profit
housing developers who wish to divest and to provide badly-needed social
housing more quickly and with less risk to their financial stability; and

12. This could be achieved by amending the DCL By-Law to allow non-profit housing
providers who purchase recently completed buildings to be eligible for a refund of
the amount of DCLs and CACs paid by the original for-profit developer.

Standing Committee of Council on Policy and Strategic Priorities
Minutes, Wednesday, January 21, 2026 10

THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED

A. THAT Council directs staff to explore, and report back on, options to create a
streamlined mechanism that allows a refund of Development Cost Levies (DCLs)
and Community Amenity Contributions (CACs) be paid to non-profit housing
organizations when they purchase a development, for the purpose of providing
social housing, that was originally designated for market housing, and was
therefore charged DCLs and CACs. As long as the non-profit organization would
have been exempt had it developed the project originally.

B. THAT Council directs staff to consider how such a mechanism might interact with
zoning rules, and how acquisition and conversion to social housing might trigger
additional regulatory steps, particularly around potential requirements for new
public hearings. Where these additional steps exist, Council directs staff to
present options to streamline and truncate approvals processes for these
projects where the only change proposed to the original approval is the level of
housing affordability required to be met by the new owner of the project and
associated or incidental changes.

C. THAT Council directs staff to analyze and report back on funding mechanisms,
such as the Empty Homes Tax reserve, that could support extended time-frame
reimbursements without creating disruption to existing City funding commitments
or requiring approval of City Council.

D. THAT Council directs staff to identify and report back on any changes which
would need to be made to the Vancouver Charter to effect streamlined
mechanism options for refunds of DCLs.
summary: Directs staff to study streamlined levy refunds and approvals when non-profit providers acquire market developments for social housing.
rationale: The minutes identify a detailed study and report-back request, but the bounded excerpt is marked truncated.

agenda_description: Good Pay for Good People's Work: Recertifying Vancouver as a Living Wage Employer
motion_group_title: Good Pay for Good People's Work: Recertifying Vancouver as a Living Wage Employer
motion_text:
MOVED by Councillor Maloney
SECONDED by Councillor Fry

THAT the Committee recommend to Council

WHEREAS

1. Each year, Living Wage BC and the BC Society for Policy Solutions calculate the
Living Wage, an annual standardised calculation of the minimum hourly wage
that an individual working full time needs to earn to cover basic living expenses,
such as groceries, clothing, rent, and childcare once government taxes, credits,
deductions and subsidies are taken into account. It is a bare bones budget that
does not include debt repayment or savings for future plans;

2. Metro Vancouver’s living wage is currently $27.85 (Living Wage Report, 2025).
The figure is 80 cents higher than the preceding year’s and $10 per hour above
the provincial minimum wage;

3. In August 2016, Living Wage BC first certified the City of Vancouver as a Living
Wage Employer. Staff subsequently reported a range of “unintended positive
consequences” with some workers characterizing the policy as life changing;

4. In January 2023, after six and a half years as a certified Living Wage Employer,
the City of Vancouver withdrew from the program;

5. The need for a living wage remains acute. Between 2024 and 2025, grocery
prices increased 3.6% across Metro Vancouver. Food is the second-largest
household expense, after shelter. While housing costs have recently stabilized,
the region continues to record the highest average asking rents in Canada;

6. Across British Columbia, there are nearly 500 Living Wage employers that have
committed to ensuring their direct and contracted staff earn a living wage,
including the City of Victoria, YVR Airport and Vancity Credit Union. The total
includes 13 local governments and public bodies;

7. In a recent survey, British Columbia’s Living Wage Employers reported a range
of benefits from certification, including easier recruitment, higher employee
retention, and higher worker morale; and

8. People who work for the City of Vancouver should be able to afford to live here,
raise their kids here, and contribute to the life of their community. By paying a
Living Wage to all direct staff and contractors, the City can help foster a fairer
and more affordable city.

THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED THAT Vancouver City Council affirm its commitment to
have the City of Vancouver be re-certified as a living wage employer by Living Wage BC

Standing Committee of Council on Policy and Strategic Priorities
Minutes, Wednesday, January 21, 2026 4

and direct staff to report back by Q2 2026 on the steps necessary to become re-certified
as a Living Wage employer.
summary: Proposes recertifying Vancouver as a living-wage employer and requesting a staff report on necessary steps.
rationale: The exact minutes excerpt clearly states the proposed recertification commitment and report-back direction.

agenda_description: Motion 7. Supporting a Fare-Free Transit Route Pilot in Vancouver
motion_group_title: Motion 7. Supporting a Fare-Free Transit Route Pilot in Vancouver
motion_text:
MOVED by Councillor Orr
SECONDED by Councillor Fry

THAT the Committee recommend to Council

WHEREAS

1. The cost of transit fares can pose a barrier to mobility for low-income individuals,
seniors, and families in Vancouver, limiting their access to employment,
education, health care, and other essential services;

2. In January 2019, Vancouver City Council endorsed the #AllOnBoard campaign,
which urged TransLink to implement free transit for youth and a sliding-scale fare
system for low-income residents, underscoring the City’s commitment to
improving transit affordability and equity;

3. Improving transit affordability and access supports the City’s climate and
transportation goals by encouraging a shift from private vehicles to public transit,
thereby reducing greenhouse gas emissions and traffic congestion;

4. New York City ran a successful free transit pilot from September of 2023 until
September of 2024, targeting five bus routes, one in each borough. The results
of the pilot were very positive:

a. A 30 percent increase in ridership on weekdays and 38 percent on
weekends;

b. Assaults on bus operators dropped by 38.9 percent;

c. 11% of new riders transitioned from car or taxi to public transit;

d. The largest increase in new riders was from individuals earning less than
$28,000;

5. Fare-free pilots based on route have been implemented in Kansas City, MO, and
Boston, MA, and fare-free bus systems have been successfully implemented in
Olympia, WA, Albuquerque, NM, Richmond, VA, Orangeville, ON, Luxembourg,
and elsewhere;

Standing Committee of Council on City Finance and Services
Minutes, Wednesday, December 10, 2025 33

6. Several major bus routes in Vancouver, including Route 3 (Main Street), Route 9
(Broadway), Route 20 (Victoria Drive), and Route 41 (41st Avenue), are well
used, serve diverse communities (including many lower-income neighborhoods),
and are iconic parts of the transit network. These routes’ popularity and citywide
significance make them strong candidates for a high-visibility fare-free transit
pilot that could maximize public awareness and ridership impact; and

7. TransLink (the regional transportation authority) is responsible for transit
operations and fare policy in Metro Vancouver, and any fare-free transit initiative
within the city will require collaboration with TransLink to design and implement
the pilot effectively.

THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED

A. THAT Vancouver City Council direct staff to seek to work with TransLink to
identify and evaluate options for implementing a one year fare-free transit pilot on
two or three bus routes or corridors across the City of Vancouver, including
consideration of, but not limited to, Route 5 (Robson Street), Route 9
(Broadway), Route 20 (Victoria Drive), and Route 41 (41st Avenue).

B. THAT in evaluating potential routes for the fare-free pilot, staff consider criteria
aimed at maximizing public benefit and feasibility, including:

1. Equity Impact - prioritizing routes that would provide the greatest benefit
to lower-income residents, seniors, and families by improving access to
affordable transportation in their daily lives;

2. Symbolic and Popular Routes - focusing on routes that are iconic or
heavily used in Vancouver’s transit network (such as the 5, the 20, the 9,
and the 41) in order to generate broad public interest, support, and
awareness of the pilot;

3. Capacity and Congestion Relief - identification of routes that have
available unused capacity even during peak hours, and proposals for
routes that have the potential to divert some riders from overcrowded
routes into alternatives, thereby relieving peak-time congestion;

4. Geographic distribution - the recommendation of complimentary routes
that service different areas of the city, sharing the benefits of fare-free
transit.

C. THAT Council directs staff to request from TransLink cost estimates for each
fare-free pilot scenario identified, including the expected lost fare revenue and
any additional operating or administrative costs, in order to understand the
financial implications of implementing a fare-free route or corridor on a pilot
basis.

D. THAT staff be directed to inquire with TransLink whether the agency would be
willing to participate in a cost-sharing arrangement to support any of the
proposed fare-free pilot routes or corridors, such as through a contribution of

Standing Committee of Council on City Finance and Services
Minutes, Wednesday, December 10, 2025 34

transit operating funds or other resources, and to incorporate TransLink’s position
on fare-free transit routes and potential cost-sharing in the analysis and options
presented.

E. THAT Council request that the Mayor write a letter to the Province to strongly
advocate for a partnership to advance a temporary pilot program for fare-free
transit routes across Vancouver and the Lower Mainland.

F. THAT staff report back to Council with the results of the above evaluation and
collaboration, including options for recommended route(s) for the fare-free transit
pilot, the estimated revenue loss and other costs associated with each option,
and any opportunities for partnership or funding support from TransLink by Q2 of
2026 in order for Council to consider next steps toward implementing the fare-
free transit route pilot in Vancouver.
summary: Proposes evaluating a one-year fare-free bus-route pilot with TransLink, including routes, equity, costs, funding partnerships, and a report back.
rationale: The exact minutes excerpt fully describes the proposed evaluation, collaboration, advocacy, and report back.

motion_text:
FINAL MOTION AS APPROVED

WHEREAS

1. The City of Vancouver currently relies on the microblogging website X.com
(formerly Twitter) as the primary platform for real-time online updates on Council
agendas and speaker lists;

Standing Committee of Council on City Finance and Services
Minutes, Wednesday, December 10, 2025 31

2. Sole reliance on X.com for real time online updates poses accessibility
challenges for residents who do not use or cannot access the platform;

3. Residents who do not consent to creating an account with X.com are unable to
see real-time updates. For instance, the @VanCityClerk account displays content
only up to December 2024 for viewers without an X.com account 3 4;

4. Creating an X.com account requires users share personal information like email
and phone number, and grant X worldwide license to use, copy, and reproduce
their content, including the right to use their content to train its AI model, Grok;

5. Research indicates X.com promotes disinformation and misinformation, fosters
political polarization, may be involved in election interference, and amplifies
divisive narratives, undermining the neutrality expected of official government
communications 5;

6. Recent controversies involving Grok, X.com’s AI chatbot, producing antisemitic
and extremist outputs, misidentifying public figures and misrepresenting factual
information raises reputational and ethical concerns for public institutions using
the platform 6 7 8;

7. Following the interest in Vancouver’s 2026 budget, many of the 639 registered
speakers expressed frustration that X.com was the only means available to them
for tracking real-time schedule updates; and

8. Numerous open-source and third-party APIs exist to provide micro-blogging that
can be embedded on the official city website, either as server-side or client-side
integrated solution: including RSS and XML feeds, JavaScript widgets, and/or
government-grade meeting management platforms to integrate micro-blogging
real-time updates.

THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED
